card.rationale: Matches students who are strong in biology, chemistry, or physics and who want to care for people and understand the human body.

card.careerReality: [VERIFY] Medicine opens paths in clinical practice, public health, and research in Nigeria and abroad. Entry is highly competitive.
card.honestRisks: Very competitive entry. Long training path. Choosing Medicine only for prestige rather than genuine interest in people and science is a common regret.

worryThemes.reassurance: Family opinions come from love, not always knowledge. Hodos is designed to help you have that conversation — the Parent Mode summary gives your family the same honest picture you have. Many students who talked it through with their parents found their family was more open than expected once they had real information to discuss.

Cost is a real factor, not a reason to avoid your best fit. The limit notes in your brief flag specific financial planning steps for each course — check them. Scholarships, federal vs state university fees, and part-time income during study are all worth researching before ruling anything out.

Uncertainty at this stage is completely normal — it is a sign you are taking the decision seriously. No tool removes all doubt, and Hodos is not a verdict. Use this brief as a starting point: talk to people actually working in the fields that interest you, and treat the 'questions for a professional' section of each card as a real to-do.

Nigerian graduate employment varies significantly by field and by the skills you bring. The brief includes a Nigerian career reality section for each course — it gives you an honest picture of local entry points without invented statistics. The skills-to-stack section points at what actually differentiates graduates in each field.

Most students who succeed in demanding courses were not certain they could at the start. The honest risks section of each course card tells you what actually trips students up — forewarned is forearmed. Talk to someone in the field and ask them directly: 'What kind of student does well here?' Their answer will tell you more than any ranking.

parentDiscussionStarters.cost: Have you and your child talked through how the programme will be funded — including professional exam fees and living costs? It would be worth researching scholarship and bursary options together.
parentDiscussionStarters.close_to_home: Your child has indicated they would prefer to study close to home. Would you like to look together at which accredited institutions offering their top choices are nearby?
parentDiscussionStarters.shorter: Your child has flagged a preference for a shorter programme. The notes in each course card include programme length — it may be worth discussing together which length feels right given your family's situation.
parentDiscussionStarters.earn_sooner: Your child has noted they want to start earning relatively soon after graduation. The career reality notes for each course give an honest picture of typical time-to-employment — a useful starting point for that conversation.
parentDiscussionStarters.family_expects: Your child has noted that family expectations are a factor. This summary is not a verdict — it is the starting point for an open conversation. The courses here are the ones that fit your child's actual strengths and interests, framed honestly for you to discuss together.
parentDiscussionStarters.abroad: Your child is interested in studying or working abroad in the future. The notes in each course card flag international portability — it may be worth discussing what that path realistically looks like.
parentDiscussionStarters.scholarship: Your child has noted they will need a scholarship or financial aid. Each course card includes a note on scholarship routes — researching these together early would be a good next step.
parentDiscussionStarters.balance: Your child has flagged the importance of personal time and balance. The honest risks section for each course card includes a realistic note on workload — worth discussing openly.

nextStepsChecklist: Confirm your JAMB subject combination with an official source (jamb.gov.ng).
Speak to at least one person currently working in each field you are considering.
Check programme duration and entry requirements at your target universities.
Research available scholarships and bursaries if cost is a factor.
Visit an open day or faculty event before making a final decision.
